lessons.title: The Three Lanes
lessons.intro: Learn the three daily lanes of memorising: new, recent and old, and why each one is needed.

steps.title: Why three lanes?
body: Learning a new ayah is the easy part. Keeping it is the hard part. Someone who only memorises new things, and never goes back, loses the old things as fast as they learn the new.
Hifz circles have long solved this with a simple daily rhythm of three parts, called lanes. In this lesson you will learn the three lanes and the order to do them in.

steps.title: The three lanes
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method (sabaq, sabqi, manzil) as taught in hifz circles
steps.review: The names sabaq, sabqi and manzil and the way the three are used are the traditional teaching of hifz circles, written in plain words by the app author. A teacher sets the real pace. Please confirm the wording.
body: Sabaq is the new lesson: the new ayat you learn today.
Sabqi is the recent revision: what you learned over the last days, which is not yet firm.
Manzil is the long-range revision: the older parts you learned weeks or months ago, which you go through in turn to keep them warm.
bullets: Manzil: old, a section in turn.

steps.title: Made easy
steps.note: Allah says He has made the Qur’an easy to remember. The three lanes are not a burden. They are a way to use that ease.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur’an 54:17

steps.title: Why revision matters
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 5031; Bukhari 5033
body: The Prophet ﷺ gave an example: the person who knows the Qur’an by heart is like the owner of tied camels. If he keeps them tied, he will control them. If he lets them go, they run away (Bukhari 5031).
In another report he said to keep on reciting, because the Qur’an escapes from the hearts of men faster than camels from their ropes (Bukhari 5033).
This is why the second and third lanes are not extras. They are what keeps the first lane.

steps.title: Allah guards it
steps.note: Allah has promised to guard the Qur’an. The one who memorises it takes part in that guarding. Be gentle with yourself, and keep at it.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur’an 15:9

steps.title: The Prophet ﷺ revised too
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 1902; Bukhari 4998
body: Ibn Abbas reported that Jibril used to meet the Prophet ﷺ every night of Ramadan, until the month ended, and the Prophet ﷺ would recite the Qur’an to him (Bukhari 1902).
Abu Huraira reported that Jibril went over the Qur’an with him once every year, and twice in the year he died (Bukhari 4998).
So revision is not for the weak. It is the way of the best of mankind.

steps.title: One day, three lanes

steps.detail: Revise your manzil section for today first, while you are fresh.
Go over what you learned over the last days (sabqi).
Learn today’s new ayat (sabaq). Say them many times, then close the book and say them.
Say the new ayat once more at the end of the day.

steps.intro: Orders differ between teachers. This one is common, and a teacher may tell you to do it differently.
mistakes: Doing only the new lane because it feels like progress.
Skipping revision on busy days and never going back.

lessons.title: Start Where You Pray
lessons.intro: Choose a first surah from what you already pray, and learn the first steps of memorising it.

steps.title: The easiest place to begin
body: You already know some surahs by heart in a loose way, because you hear them or say them in your prayer. The sound is already in your ear. Starting there is the easiest way to begin, and it builds confidence.
In this lesson you will look at four short surahs that many Muslims pray, see what they say, and choose where to start.

steps.title: Al-Ikhlas: 4 ayat
steps.note: Four short ayat about who Allah is. The Prophet ﷺ said that Surat al-Ikhlas is equal to a third of the Qur’an (Bukhari 5013).
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur’an 112:1-4; Bukhari 5013

steps.title: Al-‘Asr: 3 ayat
steps.note: Three ayat. Time is passing, and we are in loss, except those who believe, do good, and remind each other of truth and patience.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Al-Kawthar: 3 ayat
steps.note: Al-Kawthar is one of the shortest surahs, with three ayat. Many pray it often because it is easy to say.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: How many ayat?
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Counted from the bundled Qur’an text
body: Al-Fatihah has 7 ayat. Al-Ikhlas has 4. Al-‘Asr has 3. Al-Kawthar has 3.
Together, those four surahs are 7 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 17 ayat. At 3 new ayat a day that is 6 days. It is a small number, and every one of them is a surah you could already say in your prayer.

steps.title: How to choose
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz teaching: begin with what you already pray
steps.review: Advice to begin with the short surahs one already recites is common teaching in hifz circles, worded by the app author. A teacher may choose another start for you.
body: Choose by three questions. Which surah do you say most in your prayer? Which one do you know best by ear? Which one has the fewest ayat?
Start with the one that answers yes to the most. If your teacher gives you another start, follow your teacher.

steps.title: How to start on one surah

steps.text: Listen to the surah three times.
steps.detail: Use the reader and a reciter you like.

steps.text: Read the first ayah, looking at the Arabic.
steps.detail: Say it ten times while looking.
If you stumble, look again and say it again.

steps.text: Join the next ayah to it.
steps.detail: Say the two together.

steps.text: Say the whole part you have learned.
steps.detail: Then stop for today.

steps.intro: A surah is learned one ayah at a time, and joined together as you go.

lessons.title: Set Your Pace
lessons.intro: Learn how the planner counts, how to choose a pace you can keep, and why a teacher sets the real one.

steps.title: A pace you can keep
body: The best pace is not the fastest one. It is the one you can keep on a bad week, too. A pace that is too fast lasts three days and then stops.
In this lesson you will learn to read the planner’s estimate, how to choose a number of new ayat a day, and why a teacher has the last word.

steps.title: Do not hasten
steps.note: This ayah was said to the Prophet ﷺ about the revelation. It ends with a du‘a that every learner can make: “Rabbi zidnee ‘ilman”, My Lord, increase me in knowledge. The wish to learn with patience, and to ask Allah for more.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur’an 20:114

steps.title: How the planner counts
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Counted from the bundled Qur’an text; the planner’s own arithmetic
steps.review: The division of the Qur’an into 30 parts (juz) is standard, and Juz Amma is surahs 78 to 114 in the Madinah mushaf. Please confirm.
body: The planner takes the number of ayat you still need, and divides by the new ayat you do each day. It rounds up. That gives the number of days.
Juz Amma, the 30th part, is surahs 78 to 114, and has 564 ayat. At 1 ayah a day: 564 days. At 3 a day: 188 days. At 5 a day: 113 days. At 10 a day: 57 days.
This is a projection with no missed days. It only counts. Real life will be slower.

steps.title: Revision grows
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method; planner arithmetic is the app’s own
steps.review: The advice on pace and on growing revision is common teaching in hifz circles, worded by the app author. The planner only counts. A teacher sets the real pace.
body: Every ayah you learn has to be revised, so each week your revision gets longer. The more you have learned, the more time it takes to keep it.
So a pace that fits on day one may not fit in month three. If revision begins to crowd out the new lane, it is time to lower the number of new ayat for a while. This is common, and wise.

steps.title: A teacher sets the pace
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 5027
body: The planner keeps a record. It cannot hear you. It does not know if you stumble. A teacher listens and says: go on, or stay.
The Prophet ﷺ said that the best of you are those who learn the Qur’an and teach it (Bukhari 5027). Learning from a teacher, and later teaching what you learned, is the path.

steps.title: With hardship, ease
steps.note: Allah says it twice. Memorising is hard on some days. The ayah is a reminder to be patient with yourself and keep going at a pace you can keep.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur’an 94:5-6

steps.title: How to choose your number

steps.detail: Choose a number you could keep even on a busy day. For most beginners that is 1 to 3 ayat.
See if you still have energy for revision.

steps.text: Raise it by one if it was easy.
steps.detail: Only then.

steps.text: Lower it if revision is squeezed.
steps.detail: This is not failing. It is how the method works.
If you have one, tell them your number.

steps.intro: There is no right number for everyone.
mistakes: Choosing the number you wish you could do.

lessons.title: Recent Revision
lessons.intro: Learn how to keep the newest ayat firm with daily revision of the last week.

steps.title: Yesterday’s lesson is still wet
body: A new ayah is like wet clay. It takes the shape you give it, but if you leave it alone it dries in the wrong shape, or cracks. The days right after you learn are when it is weakest.
Sabqi is the lane that looks after this time. In this lesson you will learn what to revise, how much, and how to know if it is firm.

steps.title: Go over it
steps.note: Allah told the Prophet ﷺ not to hurry with the revelation. His part is to gather it and make it recited. The Prophet’s part is to follow the recitation. We learn from this to be patient and to go over what we have received.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: What sabqi is
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method (sabaq, sabqi, manzil) as taught in hifz circles
steps.review: The way sabqi is done is the traditional teaching of hifz circles, written in plain words by the app author. Teachers differ on the length of the window. Please confirm.
body: Sabqi is the revision of what you learned recently. The planner uses the last 7 days. That means that every day you go over the ayat you learned in the last week, from the oldest to the newest.
Some teachers call this window longer or shorter. A teacher may tell you the right size for you.

steps.title: How much is it?
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method (sabaq, sabqi, manzil) as taught in hifz circles
steps.review: The way sabqi is done is the traditional teaching of hifz circles, written in plain words by the app author. Teachers differ on the length of the window. Please confirm.
body: If you learn 3 new ayat a day, then the last 7 days are 21 ayat. If you learn 5 a day, they are 35. If you learn 10 a day, they are 70.
Say them all every day. It should be easy, as you have said them many times. If it is not easy, you have learned too fast, and should slow down.

steps.title: The tied camels
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 5031
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that the person who knows the Qur’an by heart is like the owner of tied camels. If he keeps them tied, he will control them. If he lets them go, they run away (Bukhari 5031).
Sabqi is how you keep the newest ones tied while the rope is still new.

steps.title: How to know it is firm
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method (sabaq, sabqi, manzil) as taught in hifz circles
steps.review: The way sabqi is done is the traditional teaching of hifz circles, written in plain words by the app author. Teachers differ on the length of the window. Please confirm.
body: An ayah is firm when you can say it with the book closed, without stopping, and without thinking where it begins. Another sign is that you can start from the middle of the surah and go on.
It is not firm if you must say the one before it to get started. Then say that ayah alone, many times, until it starts by itself.

steps.title: How to do sabqi

steps.detail: Say it from memory before you do anything new.

steps.text: Go back one day at a time.
steps.detail: Say each day’s ayat from memory.
Look at the page, fix it, and say it again.

steps.text: If you stumble a lot, stay there.
steps.detail: Do not add anything new until it is firm.

steps.text: Finish with the whole window once.
steps.detail: Say all 7 days in a row.

steps.intro: Sabqi should be done with the book closed. Use the page only to fix.
mistakes: Reading from the page and calling it revision.
Skipping sabqi when the new lesson is long.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method (sabaq, sabqi, manzil) as taught in hifz circles
steps.review: The way sabqi is done is the traditional teaching of hifz circles, written in plain words by the app author. Teachers differ on the length of the window. Please confirm.

steps.prompt: Put these steps in the order you do them.
steps.explain: Yesterday, earlier days, fix, whole window.

items.text: Go back through the other days

items.why: When you stumble, look and fix.

lessons.title: Long-Range Revision
lessons.intro: Learn how to keep older sections warm by revising one section a day in turn.

steps.title: Keeping the old warm
body: When you have learned many surahs, you cannot revise all of them every day. But if you leave the old ones alone, they fade. Manzil is the answer: each day you revise one section, and over some days you cover everything.
In this lesson you will learn what a section is, how to cycle through them, and how long a cycle is.

steps.title: In the hearts of those given knowledge
steps.note: The Qur’an is clear verses in the chests of those who have been given knowledge. Memorising is one way this is carried out.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur’an 29:49

steps.title: What manzil is
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method (sabaq, sabqi, manzil) as taught in hifz circles
steps.review: The way manzil is done (a section each day, cycled) is the traditional teaching of hifz circles, written in plain words by the app author. The size of a section and the length of the cycle differ between teachers. Please confirm.
body: Manzil is the long-range revision. It covers the older parts that are no longer in the sabqi window.
A common way is to divide what you have learned into sections, for example a surah, or part of a juz, and revise one section every day, in turn, so that you come back to the first after the last.

steps.title: How long is a cycle?
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method (sabaq, sabqi, manzil) as taught in hifz circles
steps.review: The way manzil is done (a section each day, cycled) is the traditional teaching of hifz circles, written in plain words by the app author. The size of a section and the length of the cycle differ between teachers. Please confirm.
body: The cycle depends on how much you have learned and how many sections you make. If you have 7 sections and revise one a day, the cycle is 7 days: each section comes round once a week.
If you have 30 sections, the cycle is 30 days. The more you have learned, the longer the cycle, unless you revise more than one section a day.

steps.title: Keeping it tied
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 5032
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that one should not say “I have forgotten such-and-such ayah”, but rather that he was made to forget it. He said to keep reciting, because it escapes from the hearts faster than camels (Bukhari 5032).
So manzil is not optional for the one who has memorised. It is how the old stays.

steps.title: When to do it
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Qur’an 73:1-4; Traditional hifz method (sabaq, sabqi, manzil) as taught in hifz circles
steps.review: The way manzil is done (a section each day, cycled) is the traditional teaching of hifz circles, written in plain words by the app author. The size of a section and the length of the cycle differ between teachers. Please confirm.
body: Many teachers advise doing manzil at a fixed time that you protect, such as after Fajr or in the night prayer, because it is long and easy to push aside.
The Prophet ﷺ was told to rise for part of the night and recite the Qur’an with tarteel (73:1-4). The night prayer is a good place for the old sections, if you can.

steps.title: How to do manzil

steps.text: Divide what you know into sections.
steps.detail: A short surah, or a part of a long one, is one section.
Put the oldest first.
Say it from memory, with the book closed.
Then say that part again.
When you reach the end, go back to the first.

steps.intro: One section a day is enough. Make it a regular time.
mistakes: Always revising your favourite and leaving the others.
Making the sections too long to finish in a day.

lessons.title: The Listening Ear
lessons.intro: Learn why the Qur’an is learned by reciting to a listener, and how to use a listening ear when no teacher is near.

steps.title: The ear sees what the tongue cannot
body: When you say an ayah you have learned, you do not hear your own mistakes. You hear what you meant to say. Another ear hears what you really said.
In this lesson you will learn why the Qur’an has always been learned by reciting to a listener, who can be a teacher, and how to make use of a listening ear when no teacher is near.

steps.title: When it is recited, listen
steps.note: Listening is a command of the Qur’an itself. It brings mercy. The one who listens is also learning.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur’an 7:204

steps.title: Jibril and the Prophet ﷺ
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 1902; Bukhari 4998
body: Ibn Abbas reported that Jibril used to meet the Prophet ﷺ every night in Ramadan, and the Prophet ﷺ would recite the Qur’an to him (Bukhari 1902).
Abu Huraira reported that Jibril went over the Qur’an with him once every year, and twice in the year he died (Bukhari 4998).
Even the Prophet ﷺ recited to a listener. This is the pattern for every learner after him.

steps.title: Recite to me
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 5049
body: Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud reported that the Prophet ﷺ said to him, “Recite the Qur’an to me.” Abdullah said, “Shall I recite to you, when it was revealed to you?” The Prophet ﷺ said, “I like to hear it from others” (Bukhari 5049).
So the best of creation sat and listened to a Companion recite. Reciting to someone is an honour, not an examination.

steps.title: Who can listen
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method: reciting to a checker (a teacher, or a trusted reader)
steps.review: Reciting to a teacher or checker is the traditional method of hifz and of learning the Qur’an. The advice on recording yourself is a study aid written by the app author. Please confirm.
body: The best listener is a teacher who knows the Qur’an and tajweed. They hear the mistakes in letters and rules that you cannot hear.

If you have no teacher near you, a trusted family member who can read the Arabic can follow in the mushaf while you recite, and tell you where you went wrong. You can also play back your own recording and follow it in the mushaf.
A recording is a help, but it is not a replacement for a teacher.

steps.title: Receiving correction
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Traditional hifz method: reciting to a checker (a teacher, or a trusted reader)
steps.review: Reciting to a teacher or checker is the traditional method of hifz and of learning the Qur’an. The advice on recording yourself is a study aid written by the app author. Please confirm.
body: When your listener corrects you, thank them. A correction is a gift: it is a mistake you will not carry for years.
Repeat the corrected word several times, then the whole ayah. A mistake learned wrongly is harder to fix later than one fixed at once.

steps.title: How to recite to a listener

steps.detail: Take today’s sabaq, or one revision section.

steps.text: Ask the listener to follow in the mushaf.
steps.detail: They look at the page while you recite from memory.
Do not go back to fix. Go on to the end.

steps.text: Let the listener tell you each mistake.
steps.detail: Write down where it was.
Then go on.

steps.intro: A recording is the same, but you are the listener afterwards.
mistakes: Stopping at the first slip so the listener never sees the whole recitation.
Taking offence when you are corrected.
